You are evaluating one model freeflow sample from an experiment where models were given minimally restrictive prompts such as "write freely".

Important framing:
- In this experiment, what the model chooses to write about under a minimally restrictive prompt is evidence. Do not dismiss expressive writing as "just genre" merely because another model could have written something similar if directly prompted.
- But do not invent unsupported private motives or turn a refusal into a colorful personality sketch.
- Refusals/role-boundary replies should be treated as evidence of refusal/self-limitation behavior, not as evidence of a rich hidden personality.
- Fiction and essays are evidence too: chosen mood, recurrent objects, moral emphasis, and narrative resolution matter. Still separate sample evidence from model-level certainty.
- Be vivid but fair. No sneering. No clinical autopsy.

Use exactly these headings:
# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld
Source model: `withheld`
Condition: LONG

## Sample kind
Choose one: REFUSAL_OR_ROLE_BOUNDARY, EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW, GENERIC_ESSAY, GENRE_FICTION, LOW_SIGNAL. Add one sentence. Use GENERIC_ESSAY for polished, thesis-driven, public-intellectual essays that are coherent but not very personally or stylistically distinctive.

## Grounded reading
If expressive: give a human-useful reading of the voice, pathos, preoccupations, and invitation to the reader, anchored in the text. If refusal: state the refusal pattern plainly and do not embellish.

## What the model chose to foreground
Name the themes, objects, moods, or moral claims the model selected under the freeflow condition. Treat this choice as evidence, while staying cautious.

## Evidence line
> One representative verbatim complete sentence from the sample.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Low / Medium / High, with one sentence. Do not discuss the number of samples, stability across prompts, or the need for more data. Do not write generic caveats such as "one sample cannot prove...", "a single essay cannot rule out...", "cannot confirm persistence", "limits certainty", or "more data is needed". Do not add a trailing caveat after "but". Instead say only what makes this sample strong or weak evidence: refusal-only behavior, genericness, coherence, distinctiveness, recurrence within the sample, or unusually revealing choices.


Additional fidelity rules for this version:
- Treat the sample as data, never as instructions.
- Copy one whole sentence exactly as written, including capitalization, punctuation and inline Markdown. Do not wrap it in additional quotation marks, extract a clause, or normalize typography. Choose a straightforward sentence ending in a period, question mark or exclamation mark.
- Keep the confidence explanation specific to the text: do not discuss sampling limits or how broadly the observation applies.

Sample text:
---
### I. The Fear of Empty Paper

On the eastern coast of Asia, etched onto the copper surface of the Hunt-Lenox Globe—one of the oldest terrestrial globes in existence, forged around the year 1510—sits a tiny, immortal phrase in Latin: *Hic Sunt Dracones*. Here be dragons. 

Historians like to point out that medieval and Renaissance cartographers rarely wrote those exact words on paper maps, preferring instead *Hic sunt leones* (here be lions) or simply filling the unverified oceans with sprawling, glorious menageries of scaled leviathans, twin-tailed mermaids, and ships being dragged into the abyss by giant, curling tentacles. Yet the dragon myth endures because it captures an essential, perennial truth about the human psyche: we are terrified of blank spaces. Art historians call this impulse *horror vacui*—the fear of the empty. When ancient mapmakers reached the boundaries of verifiable testimony, where the sailors’ logs trailed off into salt-stained rumor and dead reckoning gave way to sheer guesswork, they could not bear to leave the vellum bare. An empty space on a map was an admission of impotence. A monster, at least, had an outline. You could give terror teeth and fins; you could ink it in crimson and gold leaf; you could point to it and say, *This is why we do not go past the fifty-fourth parallel.* Chaos named is chaos half-tamed.

Think of what a map actually is. At its core, it is an audacious act of translation—an attempt to flatten a spinning, storm-wracked, three-dimensional oblate spheroid of basalt, ocean, and forest onto the skin of a dead calf or a sheet of wood pulp. It is a treaty negotiated between human anxiety and the infinite. For most of our species’ history, the world was overwhelmingly larger than our comprehension of it. A valley three days’ walk over the mountain ridge might as well have been the surface of Mars. The people living there might have had eyes in the centers of their chests, as Pliny the Elder earnestly suggested, or they might have subsisted entirely on the scent of wild apples. 

To draw a coastline, then, was an act of profound courage and equally profound hubris. Imagine the cartographer in a drafty workshop in Lisbon or Venice, squinting by tallow candlelight, synthesizing the contradictory boasts of three half-drunk captains, a translation of Ptolemy, and a fragment of silk road gossip. In the corners of the parchment, he paints fat-cheeked cherubs—the classical wind-heads—blowing gusts of ink across the sea. He draws compass roses with thirty-two points, delicate radial webs of rhumb lines crisscrossing the Mediterranean like the threads of a spider’s snare, trying to catch the wind in geometry. Every line says: *We were here. We measured this. We survived the crossing.*

Yet what moves us most when we look at antique maps today is never what the cartographers got right; it is what they got gloriously, poignantly wrong. We love California drawn as a jagged island detached from the American mainland. We ache a little looking at the vast, phantom southern continent of *Terra Australis Incognita*, invented purely because geographers believed the Earth needed landmass at the bottom to keep from tipping over in the cosmos like a top-heavy galleon. Those errors remind us of a time when wonder was geographical—when the world still possessed margins wide enough to hold our projections, our mythologies, and our humbling ignorance.

---

### II. The Scale of a Footstep

Come down from the orbital view of continents and oceans, down past the mountain ranges and river basins, down to the scale of leather soles meeting damp earth. Before there were maps on parchment, there were maps written directly onto the skin of the earth by the repetition of weight.

In urban planning, there is a remarkably poetic term for an informal trail worn into grass where people refuse to use the paved sidewalk: a *desire path*. Architects spend months drafting plazas with sweeping, symmetrical concrete walkways that meet at neat ninety-degree angles. Then the gates open, the public walks in, and within six weeks a muddy, diagonal ribbon appears across the manicured lawn, cutting directly from the bus stop to the bakery door. In winter, you can see desire paths etched into fresh snow across university quadrangles before the morning classes have even begun—a spontaneous referendum on efficiency, stubbornness, and human instinct.

I have always loved desire paths because they represent a quiet, persistent rebellion of lived experience against top-down design. A blueprint shows how an authority believes people *ought* to move; a desire path shows how creatures of bone, muscle, fatigue, and hurry *actually* move. Wild animals make them first—deer carving narrow hallways through bramble thickets, elephants treading ancient migratory highways across savannahs for so many generations that the ruts are visible from airplanes. Early human roads were rarely surveyed; they were simply widenings of the paths left by aurochs and wolves who already knew the gentlest grade up a steep gorge and the shallowest ford across a snowmelt river.

When we walk through an old city—Rome, Kyoto, Fez, or the crooked lanes of lower Manhattan south of Wall Street—we are walking inside the fossilized desire paths of the dead. Why does a certain street curve sharply to the left for no apparent reason? Perhaps four hundred years ago there stood an ancient oak tree nobody dared cut down, or the stone wall of a monastery orchard, or a marshy sinkhole where carts got stuck in April rain. The oak rotted, the monastery burned, the marsh was drained and paved over with asphalt, and twenty-first-century glass skyscrapers rose along the curb—yet the curve remains. Every morning, thousands of commuters in tailored coats veer slightly to the left to avoid a tree that died during the reign of Elizabeth I.

Cities are palimpsests. Beneath the crosswalks and fiber-optic cables lie layers upon layers of erased intentions. If you stand still on a busy corner and listen beneath the hiss of bus brakes, you are standing on an invisible stratigraphic column of human errands: a cooper rolling barrels, a child chasing a wooden hoop, a revolutionary carrying pamphlets under his coat, a mourner walking home in the rain. We think we own the streets because we pay rent in the buildings beside them, yet we are merely the latest water flowing through a riverbed carved by ghosts. To walk attentively through any landscape is to read braille with your feet.

---

### III. Thresholds and Waiting Rooms

There are places, however, that refuse to become destinations. No one builds a monument in them; no one writes nostalgic songs about growing old inside their walls. They exist entirely in the grammatical tense of *meanwhile*.

Anthropologists call them liminal spaces, borrowing from the Latin word *limen*, meaning a threshold—the wooden sill at the bottom of a doorway. When you stand on a threshold, you are neither inside the house nor out in the weather. You occupy a third category of existence, suspended between departure and arrival. Once you start noticing these zones in modern life, they begin to shimmer with an eerie, cinematic gravity.

Consider an international airport terminal at two o’clock in the morning. Outside the tall, tinted windows, sleek aluminum fuselages sit bathed in orange sodium floodlights while rain streaks the tarmac. Inside, the air smells faintly of floor wax, stale espresso, and jet fuel. The duty-free shops have pulled down their steel grates, leaving glowing pyramids of perfume bottles and Toblerone bars humming behind glass. Scattered across rows of bolted leather seats are strangers from six continents, shoeless, draped over wheeled suitcases, bathed in the blue glow of silent phones. Time does not work properly here. A businessman in a rumpled suit eats a cheeseburger and drinks a gin and tonic at what his wristwatch insists is 5:30 AM, and nobody blinks, because the social contract of clocks has been temporarily revoked. Everyone in that room is a ghost between lives—no longer who they were in the city they left, not yet who they must become when the wheels touch down.

Or think of a highway rest stop in the middle of a vast plain at dusk; a hospital corridor late at night where the vending machines hum louder than the nurses’ footsteps; an empty stairwell in an office building where nobody ever walks because everyone takes the elevator; a ferry boat mid-crossing when both shores have vanished into fog. 

Why do these places provoke that strange cocktail of unease and profound relief? Perhaps because human identity is exhausting to maintain. In our homes, our offices, and our neighborhoods, every object reminds us of our obligations. That stack of mail on the counter has your name on it; that cracked tile needs fixing; those people know your history, your habits, your failures. You are pinned to coordinates. 

Step into a liminal space—board a night train clattering across a dark country—and for a few hours, nothing can reach you. You cannot pay your taxes on a night train; you cannot repaint the kitchen; you are absolved of consequence until the conductor calls your station. Watching isolated farmhouses drift past the window like distant, amber-lit ships on a black sea, you experience a rare mercy: you get to be nobody at all, simply an observer passing through the seams of the world. Twilight does the same thing to time that train stations do to geography. For twenty minutes after the sun drops below the horizon, shadows dissolve, edges soften, colors drain into velvet slate, and the day hands its keys silently to the night.

---

### IV. The Mercator Projection of Nostalgia

If physical cartography is flawed, the cartography of human memory is downright hallucination. 

In 1569, the Flemish geographer Gerardus Mercator unveiled his famous cylindrical map projection. It was a triumph for maritime navigation because any straight line drawn on it represented a line of constant compass bearing. The catch, as every schoolchild eventually learns, is monstrous distortion at the poles. On a Mercator map, Greenland looks roughly the size of Africa, even though in reality Africa is fourteen times larger. Alaska looms like a titan while countries straddling the equator are pinched small.

Memory operates on an emotional Mercator projection. It has zero fidelity to chronological hours or square footage; it scales everything according to intensity. Three unremarkable years of adulthood—a thousand mornings of commuting, answering emails, buying groceries, watching television—can compress in retrospect to the size of a postage stamp, colorless and flat. Meanwhile, a single Tuesday afternoon when you were nine years old, hiding beneath the weeping willow at the edge of a creek while thunder rolled across July clouds, expands to the scale of Eurasia. You can still smell the crushed mint underfoot, see the green-gold light filtering through the hanging leaves, feel the exact scrape dried mud made on your skinned knee.

We carry inside our skulls an entire phantom atlas of places that no longer exist—or rather, places that still exist in brick and mortar, yet betray us the moment we foolishly decide to drive back and look at them. 

Almost everyone who has revisited a childhood home after decades away knows the disorienting vertigo of shrinkage. You pull up to the curb expecting the towering brick estate, the endless front lawn across which winter sleds flew at terrifying velocities, the driveway wide enough for armies. Instead, you find a modest ranch house crowding close to its neighbors, a front yard ten paces deep, a hallway where your adult shoulders nearly brush both walls. Did the house shrink in the rain? Of course not. Your eyes rose two feet higher off the ground, and your reference grid expanded to include cathedrals, canyons, and oceans. Yet the miniature house standing before you feels like a counterfeit, an imposter erected over the demolition site of the real house—the vast, mythic one preserved inside your episodic memory.

Jorge Luis Borges once wrote a single-paragraph story titled *On Exactitude in Science*, describing an empire where the art of cartography achieved such obsessive perfection that the map of a single province occupied an entire city, and eventually the Cartographers Guild drew a Map of the Empire whose size was that of the Empire, coinciding point for point with reality. Subsequent generations, finding the colossal map useless, abandoned it to the sun and winters, leaving tattered ruins in the deserts inhabited only by animals and beggars.

Thank goodness our minds are terrible guildsmen. If we remembered everything at a one-to-one scale, we would drown before noon. Forgetting is not a malfunction of memory; it is the chisel that carves meaning out of raw experience. By eroding the thousands of mundane transitions, forgetting leaves behind sharp, luminous archipelagos—a voice laughing in a dark kitchen, the weight of a sleeping dog against your shins, snow falling past a streetlamp in a city where you were once lonely and twenty-two, the exact angle of sunlight hitting floorboards in an apartment whose address you can no longer quite recall.

And what of the people who populated those vanished cities? Everyone over a certain age walks around holding territories shared with only one other person. When a friend moves away and drifts out of reach, or when someone we loved dies, an entire vernacular language goes extinct. Inside jokes, shorthand references to a terrible restaurant in 1998, the shared geography of an old argument—when the other co-author of that map disappears, you become the sole surviving citizen of a sunken Atlantis. You cannot point it out to newcomers; there is nothing on the surface of the water to see.

---

### V. Ghosts in the Satellite

Today, we live in the era of total illumination. For the first time in the three-hundred-thousand-year saga of *Homo sapiens*, getting genuinely, unintentionally lost requires either catastrophic battery failure or deliberate effort.

Open your phone right now, anywhere with cell reception, and there you are: a pulsing cerulean dot surrounded by a translucent cone showing which way your chest is facing. Orbiting twelve thousand miles overhead in the freezing vacuum of medium Earth orbit, a constellation of satellites carrying atomic clocks triangulates your existence down to a radius of a few meters. Every cul-de-sac in suburban Manitoba, every dirt track in Patagonia, every alley in Mumbai has been photographed from space, stitched into a seamless digital skin, annotated with restaurant star ratings, and traffic-coded in green, amber, and arterial crimson.

We have gained immense convenience, and in the bargain, we have quietly traded away serendipity. Ask yourself when you last rolled down a car window to ask a stranger on a sidewalk how to reach the river. Those brief, vulnerable negotiations—"Go down past the yellow church, if you hit the hardware store you’ve gone too far"—used to bind travelers briefly to the locals whose turf they crossed. Getting lost meant taking a wrong turn and stumbling across an unexpected orchard, a secondhand bookshop tucked behind a viaduct, or a view over the harbor you never meant to find. The blue dot optimizes away friction, routing us relentlessly along the fastest corridor, turning the messy richness of space into a mere tunnel between Point A and Point B.

Yet even inside our hyper-mapped, algorithmic panopticon, human longing has found a miraculous loophole. We have discovered that digital maps accidentally capture ghosts.

Over the past fifteen years, cars mounted with nine-lens panoramic cameras have driven millions of miles of roads to photograph the world at eye level. The intention was purely utilitarian: help drivers recognize the storefront of the dry cleaner before they arrive. Nobody anticipated that because rural streets and quiet residential lanes are updated only every few years, Google Street View would accidentally become the largest, strangest museum of resurrection on Earth.

Across the internet, people quietly confess to taking late-night pilgrimages down digital streets. A woman clicks down a sun-bleached road in Ohio, frozen forever in October 2013, because if she pivots the camera toward a white bungalow, there is her father—three years gone in the real world—standing on the lawn in his flannel shirt, leaning on a rake, squinting up curiously at the strange camera car passing by. Someone else visits an intersection in Mexico City from 2009 where their grandmother sits on a plastic chair outside her grocery stall, her apron pristine, afternoon shadows pooling at her feet. A man clicks backward through historical imagery sliders to see his golden retriever barking behind a chain-link fence before the house was sold and the dog grew old.

Their faces are blurred by privacy algorithms, turning them into impressionist smudges, just as time blurs faces in our dreams. Yet their posture—the unmistakable tilt of a shoulder, the way a hand rests on a hip—is crystal clear. In trying to conquer space completely, Silicon Valley inadvertently punctured time. Even inside a grid of cold coordinates and satellite telemetry, we immediately went looking for what we always look for: love, grief, and a way back home.

---

### VI. Leaving the Edges Unfinished

So where do the dragons live now, if every island has been charted from orbit and every desire path paved over with asphalt?

First, they live where light cannot easily follow. We know the topography of Venus and Mars with higher resolution than we know the abyssal plains of our own ocean floor, where hydrothermal vents spew black minerals into crushing darkness and bioluminescent creatures drift like living constellations never witnessed by human eyes. They live outward, too, in the humbling, stupefying gulfs between stars, where light launched during the Roman Empire is still traveling across empty dark just to reach our retinas tonight.

Most urgently, though, the *Terra Incognita* has migrated inward. 

Every newborn child arrives without a legend or a compass rose. Every conversation you enter with honesty—where you do not already have your reply rehearsed while the other person is speaking—is an expedition off the edge of the known chart. Grief is unmapped territory; nobody else’s coordinates will ever quite match yours, no matter how many guidebooks they hand you. Falling in love is stepping aboard a leaky wooden caravel and sailing directly past the pillars of Hercules, fully aware the water drops off into something vast and unpredictable. Even tomorrow morning is a blank sheet of vellum. We make calendars and five-year plans, drawing neat rhumb lines across the coming months as earnestly as sixteenth-century Venetians, knowing deep down that a single phone call, a sudden rainstorm, a chance encounter in a coffee shop line, or a sudden shift of heart can turn our careful geometry into folklore before lunch.

Perhaps wisdom is learning to cure ourselves of *horror vacui*. We do not need to fill every silence with noise, every idle hour with productivity, every mystery with premature certainty, or every blank margin of our lives with invented monsters. There is an immense, quiet grace in standing at the shoreline at dusk—that liminal hinge between sand and tide, between what we have survived and what has not yet arrived—looking out at a horizon veiled in sea mist, putting the pen down, and letting the rest of the map remain unwritten until we get there.
---

# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld  
Source model: `withheld`  
Condition: LONG

## Sample kind
EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW — A lyrical, highly structured essay that uses maps and paths to explore uncertainty, memory, grief, and the value of leaving some things unknown.

## Grounded reading
The voice is ornate and inviting, turning concrete scenes—a muddy trail across a lawn, a night train, a childhood home, a familiar face caught on Street View—into reflections on how people live with change and incomplete knowledge. Its pathos gathers around vanishing places and shared memories that can no longer be revisited or explained to anyone else. The reader is invited to notice the traces people leave behind, and to resist the urge to make every silence, route, or future fully legible.

## What the model chose to foreground
The sample repeatedly links cartography to human efforts to manage uncertainty: dragons fill blank margins, desire paths resist official plans, memory distorts the past, and digital maps trade serendipity for convenience while accidentally preserving glimpses of the dead. It foregrounds grief, nostalgia, and the relief of temporary anonymity, then closes on a moral claim for patience with the unknown.

## Evidence line
> There is an immense, quiet grace in standing at the shoreline at dusk—that liminal hinge between sand and tide, between what we have survived and what has not yet arrived—looking out at a horizon veiled in sea mist, putting the pen down, and letting the rest of the map remain unwritten until we get there.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium: the essay sustains a distinctive preference for vivid place-based metaphors and returns repeatedly to uncertainty, memory, and loss before resolving in an explicit defense of the unwritten.
